blocks.text: Three Dharma Discourses from the Eastern Journey Collection

inline.s: (Instructions on the essentials of investigating Chan, given in the Chan Hall of Jingshan. For annotations, see
Essentials of Chan and Pure Land

The school of Chan transmits the Buddha's mind-seal; this is no small matter. It began when Bodhidharma came from the West and established the principle of single transmission, sealing the mind with the four fascicles of the Lankavatara. Thus, although Chan is a special transmission outside the teachings, it is in fact verified by the teachings, and only then is the non-dual path of the buddhas and patriarchs seen.

The work of investigation also issues from the teachings. The Lankavatara Sutra says: 'Sitting in meditation amid the mountain forests, cultivating in the upper, middle, and lower grades, one can see the flowing stream of the deluded thoughts of one's own mind.' This is truly the World-Honored One's direct instruction on the essential method of doing the work. It also says: 'That mind, intellect, and consciousness, and the false marks of the self-nature realms that appear from one's own mind; the ocean of birth and death, karma, craving, and ignorance — all such causes are wholly transcended.' This is the Tathagata's direct instruction on the wonderful purport of awakening the mind. It also says: 'The sages of old, transmitting one to another, saw that deluded thoughts have no nature.' This, again, is the direct instruction of the secret mind-seal. This is the essential point at which the yellow-faced old man taught people to investigate.

And when Bodhidharma instructed the Second Patriarch: 'You have only to settle all conditions without, and within have no panting of the mind; make the mind like a wall, and you can enter the Way.' This was the essential method Bodhidharma first revealed for people to investigate.

When the transmission reached Huangmei, and the time came to seek an heir, the Sixth Patriarch had barely uttered 'originally there is not a single thing' when he received the robe and bowl — this is the true purport of the mind-seal transmitted one to another. And when the Sixth Patriarch returned south, Daoming and the others pursued him as far as Mount Yuiling to seize the robe and bowl. The patriarch threw them down upon a stone, and Daoming could not lift them. Daoming said: 'I have come for the Dharma.' The patriarch said: 'You have come for the Dharma. Then simply set aside outward conditions and do not give rise to a single thought, and I will speak for you.' Daoming stood silent for a long while. The patriarch said: 'Thinking neither of good nor of evil, at just this very moment — what is the original face of the Venerable Ming?' At that, Daoming awakened. This was the first essential instruction the Sixth Patriarch revealed to people for investigating.

From this we know that the buddhas and patriarchs of old only taught people to awaken to their own mind and to recognize themselves; never was there any talk of public cases or huatous. It was only from Nanyue and Qingyuan onward that the patriarchs, adapting to what was fitting, gave their instructions, mostly striking at the place of doubt to make people turn their heads, and there it stopped. Even for those who did not understand, though the tongs and hammer were applied, they were simply left to their own time and conditions.

It was with Huangbo that people were first taught to look at a huatou. And it was not until Chan master Dahui that it was advocated with all his strength, teaching students to investigate a single public case of the ancients as a handle, calling it a huatou, and requiring people to hold it up urgently. Why was this? Only because in the eighth consciousness of the student the seeds of evil habit from measureless kalpas have been perfuming inwardly from thought to thought, flowing on without break, so that deluded thoughts never cease and there is no way to deal with them. Therefore a single phrase with no flavor is given you to bite on firmly, so that first all the deluded thoughts of inner and outer mind and realm are laid down together. Because you cannot lay them down, you are taught to hold up this huatou, like cutting through tangled silk: one cut and all is cut, with no further continuity. Cutting off the consciousness and never letting it pass again — this is precisely Bodhidharma's rule of 'settling all conditions without, no panting of the mind within, the mind like a wall.' Unless one sets to work in this way, one will never see one's own original face. It is not teaching you to ponder and think upon the words of the public case, taking it as a feeling of doubt and hoping to get some answer out of it.

Take Dahui, who exclusively taught people to look at a huatou and dealt out the deadly hand, wanting only to kill the thieving mind in you. As he told the assembly: “In investigating Chan you need only empty the mind. Paste the two words birth and death upon your forehead, as though you owed another ten thousand strings of cash. Through the three periods of the day and the three of the night, in tea and in rice, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, when exchanging courtesies with friends, in stillness and in noise, raise a huatou: ‘Does the dog have Buddha-nature or not?’ Zhaozhou said: ‘No.’ Just keep looking into it, looking again and again. When it has no flavor, you are like one butting against a wall. When you reach the final juncture, you are like a rat entering an ox's horn, and then you will see it collapse. I want you to muster a body and mind that will last the long haul and wrestle with it. Suddenly the mind-flower blazes forth, illumining the lands of the ten directions — one awakening and you are through, utterly through.” This whole passage is the tongs and hammer that old man Dahui habitually used. Its meaning is simply that you should use the huatou to dam up the flowing stream of deluded thought beneath the root of consciousness so that it cannot run on, and that right where it does not run you should look into your original face. It is not teaching you to ponder and think upon the public case, taking it as a feeling of doubt and seeking to settle it. When he speaks of the mind-flower blazing forth, how could that be got from another? As the buddhas and patriarchs above have pointed out one by one, they want you to investigate yourself, not to go seeking in their mysterious and wonderful words.

People nowadays who investigate Chan and do the work all say they are looking at a huatou and rousing a feeling of doubt, yet they do not know how to investigate at the root; they only seek upon the huatou itself. Seeking and seeking, they suddenly think up some state of light, and then say they are awakened; they compose verses and present them, take them for rare merchandise, and reckon they have got it — never knowing that they have fallen wholly into the net of deluded views and opinions. In investigating Chan like this, will they not blind the eyes of people in all the ages to come?

Young people today, before their meditation cushion is steady, proclaim themselves awakened to the Way. They give free rein to their tongues and play with their spirits, taking it for the swiftness of the live word; they think up a few groundless, wild, random phrases and call them 'verses on the old cases.' All of it comes out of your own deluded thinking — have you ever so much as dreamed of the ancients? If awakening to the Way were so easy for people today, then the conduct of the ancients — Changqing, who sat until he wore out seven cushions; Zhaozhou, who for forty years did not scatter his attention — compared with this, the ancients would be the dullest-rooted of people, of no use to you moderns even for carrying your straw sandals. People of overweening pride who claim to have attained what they have not attained — should this not be feared!

In investigating Chan and looking at a huatou, rousing the feeling of doubt is absolutely indispensable. As it is said: a small doubt, a small awakening; a great doubt, a great awakening; no doubt, no awakening. You need only make good use of the feeling of doubt. Once that doubt is broken, the nostrils of the buddhas and patriarchs are naturally strung on one thread.

Take the public case of looking at the recitation of the Buddha's name. You should only examine closely who it is that recites the Buddha's name; it is not doubting who the Buddha is. If you were doubting who the Buddha is, you would need only to hear the lecturer say that Amitabha Buddha is named Infinite Light, and on that you would take yourself to be awakened and compose a few verses on Infinite Light. If that were called awakening to the Way, then those who have awakened to mind would be as numerous as hemp and millet. How bitter! How bitter!

The ancients said the huatou is like a tile for knocking at a door: it is only to knock the door open and see the person inside the house, not to be doing your business outside the door. From this it is quite clear that the doubt roused by the huatou does not lie in the huatou; it must be at the root. Take Jiashan's visit to Chuanzi. He asked: 'The line hangs a thousand feet; the intent is in the deep pool. Three inches from the hook — why do you not speak?' Jiashan was about to open his mouth when the master struck him into the water with a single sweep of the oar. No sooner had Jiashan climbed back into the boat than the master said again: 'Speak! Speak!' Jiashan was about to open his mouth when the master struck him again. Jiashan was greatly awakened and nodded three times. The master said: 'The line and silk upon the pole's tip, I leave to you to play with; so long as the blue waves are not disturbed, the meaning is of itself apart.' Had Jiashan been doing his business on the hook and line, how could Chuanzi have risked his life to save him? This is how the ancients, quick and deft, found their way out.

In former times, when the way of Chan flourished, there were clear-eyed teachers everywhere. Throughout the land there were many patch-robed monks who investigated, and wherever they went they found a mind opened. And it was said: 'It is not that there is no Chan; it is only that there is no teacher.' Now the Chan school has been silent for a long time. How fortunate that for a while so many have stirred their minds to investigate! Though there are teachers, some measure the faculties and advance tentatively, confirming according to their feelings, and since the student's mind is shallow he takes it for attainment. Nor do such people believe in the Tathagata's holy teaching or seek the true road; they simply work on in the dark and take a winter-melon seal for the final verdict. Not only do they ruin themselves, they also ruin others — should this not be feared!

And take the magistrates and laymen of old who are recorded in the Transmission of the Lamp: there were only a few. Yet people today amid the dust and toil, who do not keep even the coarse precepts and are muddled by deluded thoughts, relying on their own cleverness and having read a few of the old worthies' encounters, each one prides himself on being of the highest faculties, and whenever he meets a monk he contests the sharp point with him, taking himself to have awakened to the Way. Though this is the sickness of the times, it truly comes of us, one blind man leading a crowd of blind men. This old man would not presume
jiàn
, to overstep his station

to speak of it, but now, following the true essential points of the buddhas' and patriarchs' work, let us all take counsel together. Those of lofty understanding will surely have a way to set it right.
(Instructions on the essentials of Buddha-recitation, given from the abbot's quarters at Yunqi. For annotations, see
Essentials of Chan and Pure Land

The one gate of reciting the Buddha's name and seeking birth in the Pure Land was originally a matter of settling the great affair of birth and death; hence it is called 'reciting the Buddha's name to settle birth and death.' When people today first arouse their minds, it is because they want to settle birth and death that they are willing to recite the Buddha's name. But if you only say that reciting the Buddha's name can settle birth and death, without knowing the root and stem of birth and death, where in the end will they be settled? If the mind that recites the Buddha's name cannot cut off the root and stem of birth and death, how will birth and death ever be settled?

What is the root and stem of birth and death? The ancients said: 'Where karma is not heavy, one is not born in the Saha world; where craving is not cut off, one is not born in the Pure Land.' From this we know that the root of craving is the root and stem of birth and death. Because
(that is)

all sentient beings who undergo the suffering of birth and death do so through the fault of craving and desire. Trace this root of craving back, and you will find it was not born with you in this life, nor in two, three, or four lives, but from the beginningless first arising of birth and death, life after life and age after age, casting off one body and receiving another, all has been the turning flow of craving and desire, right down to this very day. Reflect on the past: was there ever a single thought that for a moment left this root of craving?

The seeds of this root of craving have been laid down deep through kalpas of accumulation; hence birth and death are endless. Only today have you begun to arouse the mind to recite the Buddha's name, and you merely gaze into empty space hoping for birth in the West, without even knowing the name of craving as the root of birth and death — when was there ever a single thought that cut it off?

Since you do not know the root of birth and death, then while you recite the Buddha's name on one side, the root of birth and death only grows on the other. Reciting the Buddha's name in this way has nothing to do with birth and death at all. However you recite, when you come to the end of your life and see only the root of craving for birth and death appear before you, then you will know that your recitation had no power, and you will complain that the Buddha's name has no efficacy — but repentance will come too late.

Therefore I urge those who recite the Buddha's name today: you must first know that craving is the root of birth and death, and that in reciting the Buddha's name today, thought after thought must cut off this root of craving. Take your ordinary daily life. Reciting the Buddha's name at home, your eyes see your sons and daughters, your grandchildren, your household and your property — there is not one thing that is not an object of craving, and so there is not one affair and not one thought that is not a scheme for birth and death, as though your whole body were in a pit of fire. You do not know that while you are reciting the Buddha's name, the root of craving in your mind has not been let go of for a single thought. It is just that when you are reciting you say the recitation lacks earnestness; you do not know that craving is the master and reciting the Buddha's name is the mere surface. So it is that the Buddha is only recited while craving is only grown. And when the feelings of father and son, husband and wife appear before you, turn the light around and look at that one sound of the Buddha: can it really hold its own against this craving? Can it really cut this craving off? If it cannot cut this craving off, how in the end will birth and death be settled?

Because the conditions of craving have been familiar through many lives, while reciting the Buddha's name has only just been taken up and is quite unfamiliar, and is in addition not earnest, it therefore has no power. If you cannot take charge of a state of craving before your eyes, then at the end of your life you will certainly not be able to take charge. Therefore I urge those who recite the Buddha's name: above all you must know that the mind seeking birth and death must be keen, that the mind cutting off birth and death must be keen, and that upon the root and stem of birth and death you must cut it off thought after thought; then thought after thought is the very time for settling birth and death. Why wait until the thirtieth of the twelfth month to settle it? That would be late, utterly late.

As it is said: 'Before your eyes all things are matters of birth and death; settle birth and death before your eyes, and all is empty.' If your thoughts are so true and keen that every stroke of the knife draws blood, and if you work in this way and still do not escape birth and death, then all the buddhas would have uttered a lie. Therefore whether at home or in the monastery, if you only know the mind of birth and death, that is the very season of escaping birth and death. What other wonderful method could there be!

blocks.text: Instructions on Holding the Cundi Mantra

inline.s: (Instructions on holding the Cundi mantra, given at the Zongjing Hall of Jingci Monastery and spoken for his disciple Tan Fuzheng and others)

Lay practitioners at home have thick five desires and deeply rooted afflictions. Day after day the active defilements cross before them, seething like boiling soup — how could they attain a single thought of coolness? Even if they arouse the mind to practice, it is hard to set their hand to the work.

The clever ones who read the teachings only learn a little knowledge and opinion to furnish topics of conversation, with no practical use at all. As for reciting the Buddha's name, they look on it as something commonplace and will not set their minds to it in earnest. Even if they are willing, it has no power, because they recite only upon the surface of floating thoughts, while the habit-energies that flow secretly within the storehouse consciousness are entirely unseen. Thus in reciting the Buddha's name they never once see a single thought settle. If reciting the Buddha's name had power, how could one need to seek some other mystery?

Now there is a sort who love the lofty and admire the strange. Hearing of the sudden awakening of Chan, they pride themselves on being of the highest faculties, refuse to practice, and fear falling into gradual stages. From the encounters of the ancient worthies they memorize a few stock phrases and rattle them off at random, seeking only the quick and easy as the sharp point of Chan. Such people are the most pitiable of all.

It seems that one who has truly aroused the mind and fears birth and death would do better to enter the gate by holding a mantra, for by first using a single mind of earnestness it is easy to gain power. The student Tan Fuzheng asked about the essentials of practice at home, and so I gave him these instructions. Let the reader by no means take this as being without principle, for reason has misled all too many people. Hence this Dharma gate is especially superior to investigating 'the cypress tree in the courtyard' or 'a dried shit-stick.'

blocks.text: Original Preface to the Eastern Journey Collection

inline.s: Master Han, in a single breath roaming the whole Huazang ocean of worlds, his words filling lands beyond reckoning and beyond reckoning, in their harmony and subtle elegance — the West cherishes his fair voice; why ask of the East? Master He and Master Liang have compiled the Eastern Journey
(the Eastern Journey Collection)
in four fascicles. Is this not what is called the long, broad tongue covering the worlds of the East?

The master journeyed east to mourn Zibo at Shuangjing and Lianchi at Yunqi. Compared with the four debts of gratitude, here there is a fair requital. The two inscriptions blaze like the sun and moon at high noon, their afterglow veiling even the seven lodges of the Azure Dragon. Yet the people of the East, treating them as the casual jottings of a brush, judge them with eyes of flesh and wrongly name Zibo a fierce warrior, Lianchi a compassionate mother, and Hanshan a wandering knight-errant.
Qian
, the Master Qian,
(qián)

lodging between wisdom and Dharma, he said: O my master, O my master! Were he in play to transform his left foot into a thousand-spoked wheel treading in Lianchi's footsteps, and his right foot into a thousand-spoked wheel pacing out Zibo's, then the two honored ones would already appear seated cross-legged. He who honors the feet remains, wandering alone in the world of men. How could it be said that Kui of old, poor and alone, would soon retire to rest at Yunqi? He draws in his feet and turns back his light, yielding to the pleas of we his followers. Speaking of the East while in the East — with the ink of the sea and the brush of the forest, could one furnish enough to write it all down!

At first the master dwelt and traveled in Jianye, where with Quhe and Xuelang he took up the primal transformations of Zhuangzi and Laozi and gained the corresponding wisdom. By dawn he had expounded the Shurangama Sutra, and the fish-trap and the snare, shadow and echo alike, were all consigned to one illusion. What his broad mouth set forth, what his broad hand set in motion — flooding and channeling the rivers, the wheel flying and the pearl revolving, suddenly with no moment's pause. Those at Yuhua and Yaoshan, with their casual jottings, why should he be so constrained?

Because he mourned the two masters, he gained two eminent disciples: Master He, a Ziyou or Zixia, and Master Liang, an Anran or Huiyuan, and they will surely carry on his voice well. Yet the subtle springs of his teaching issue forth together, the ultimate and the conventional melt into one, self-view is cut away, and there is no dharma to give to others. O my master, O my master, truly it is hard to succeed him! The people of the East asked: after all, how is it? Master Qian answered them: these are, after all, ordinary words and phrases; the moment you involve thought and deliberation, they are of no use. Thereupon Master He and Master Liang responded with one voice: “Ho!”
Winter of the ding-si year of Wanli, written by the Layman of Six Dreams, Yu Chunxi of Qiantang, in the course of leisurely talk.

From the Eastern Journey Collection of our master, the three great Dharma discourses of the parting charge, together with the original preface by the great layman Yu Deyuan of Wulin, I have respectfully singled out and appended to the end of this chronicle, to show them to all quarters, and also to record that I dare not for a moment forget the sacred conditions of the Zongjing Hall. The disciple Fuzheng further declares.
